Alec Soth’s "Sleeping by the Mississippi" is widely regarded as one of the most influential photobooks of the 21st century. Originally published in 2004, this 2017 MACK edition is the definitive version, celebrated for restoring the book's original scale and sequence. It features 46 large-format color plates, including two "lost" images not found in the original Steidl printing.

This particular copy is hand-signed by Alec Soth on the title page, making it a cornerstone acquisition for any serious collector of modern American photography.

Condition & Specifications

  • Condition: Excellent / Near Fine (Gift-Quality).

  • Format: Hardcover, yellow cloth-bound boards.

  • Dimensions: Approx. 11" x 11.5" (28 x 30 cm).

  • Publisher: MACK, London (2017).

  • Internal State: Internal pages are crisp, bright, and untouched. The large-format color plates display exceptional tonal range and the signature "Mississippi" palette is vibrant and true.

  • Cover: The iconic yellow cloth boards are clean and vibrant. Corners are sharp and the binding is tight and square.

Collector’s Note

This MACK edition is highly prized by bibliophiles for its superior color fidelity compared to later reprints. Soth’s work—situated in the tradition of Walker Evans and Robert Frank—captures a poetic and raw "third coast" of America. A signed copy of this specific edition represents both a significant artistic document and a stable archival investment.

Archival Shipping & Handling

Given the weight and the susceptibility of the yellow cloth boards to shelf wear, this book will be handled with "white-glove" care:

  • Box-in-a-Box Method: To ensure the corners remain sharp, the book is wrapped in acid-free paper, bubble-wrapped, and shipped in a rigid, oversized box.

** SEALED + SIGNED** 1st edition//4th printing

published by Mack, 2022.
Format: Hardback
Pages: 128
Condition: New

The early settlers dubbed California ‘The Golden State’ and ‘The Land of Milk and Honey’. Today there are the obvious ironies – sprawl, spaghetti junctions and skid row – but the place is not so easily distilled or visualised, either as a clichéd paradise or as its demise. There’s a strange kind of harmony when it’s all seen together – the sublime, the psychedelic, the self-destructive. Like all places, it’s unpredictable and contradictory, but to greater extremes. Cultures and histories coexist, the beautiful sits next to the ugly, the redemptive next to the despairing, and all under a strange and singular light, as transcendent as it is harsh.

The pictures in this book begin in the desert east of Los Angeles and move west through the city, ending at the Pacific. This general westward movement alludes to a thirst for water, as well as the original expansion of America, which was born in the East and which hungrily drove itself West until reaching the Pacific, thereby fulfilling its ‘manifest’ destiny.

The people, places, and animals in the book did exist before Halpern’s camera, but he has sewn these photographs into a work of fiction or fantasy – a structure, sequence, and edit which, like Los Angeles itself, teeters on the brink of collapsing under the weight of its own strangely-shaped mass.

“This country is changing quickly… we might soon forget those interesting relics of the past that are disappearing under the redevelopment of the future.” This future is now here, and Meadows’ pictures remain as relevant as ever. Book of the Road cements the Free Photographic Omnibus as an essential document of 1970s England – an urgent and timeless visual record.

Just 21 years old when he set up the Free Photographic Omnibus, Daniel Meadows is now one of Britain’s greatest documentary photographers. He worked mostly on instinct, and many of his DIY techniques anticipate documentary media’s progress in the following decades. He remembers sewing a tape recorder into an old tweed jacket so that he could photograph while also capturing audio. The original bus – a low-bridge decker from Barton Transport – cost him just £360. Meadows’ subjects collected their free portraits the following day, after he had spent many restless hours developing film and printing in the bus’ makeshift darkroom.

Book of the Road gives readers the stories behind the photographs, from battles with angry parking attendants, nights of acute loneliness and moments of joy. This mix of images, diary entries and audio transcripts offers a unique commentary into the 1970s social climate – as well as Meadows’ mindset during the project. In Southampton in 1974 he met Florence, a part-time cleaner who he remained close with for five decades, eventually speaking at her funeral. “It was one of the great privileges of my life,” Meadows recalls.

The book offers a survey of English life when modernisation was seeping into everyday values and communities. Cobbled streets in tight-knit parishes and bustling city centres accompany familiar green pastures, but Meadows also takes us behind the curtain at marble competitions, circuses and beauty contests. Throughout, his subjects of all ages and social classes stand proudly for the camera, unaware that they were to become part of history.
